headline: Quantinuum and software firm HQS have used a trapped-ion quantum computer to simulate the nuclear magnetic resonance signal of a molecule with 22 interacting atomic nuclei.
score_reason: Credible technical benchmark, but a pre-print, and the authors say classical computers still do it better.
importance_line: Chemists and materials scientists get a sign that quantum hardware can reproduce a hard measurement, but the authors concede conventional software is still more efficient, so there is no practical advantage yet.
summary: Quantum Computing Report reports that Quantinuum, which builds trapped-ion quantum computers, and German firm HQS Quantum Simulations ran a simulation of a nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrum, the signal chemists use to work out molecular structure, on Quantinuum's H2-1 machine. They reproduced a fine double-peak feature that earlier quantum hardware tests struggled to resolve, but the authors note that classical software remains more efficient for routine work today, and the result is in a pre-print.
notes: Headline figures of 42 qubits and 1,400+ circuits are not in the article text and were left out. The molecule has 22 spins, simulated as a 21-spin effective model.
